newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Bolger launches campaign based on stability.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Bolger launches campaign based on stability.

text.p: New Zealand Prime Minister Jim Bolger launched the governing National Party's election campaign on Sunday promising stability and that "the best is yet to come".

But the latest in a series of opinion polls showed Bolger's conservatives, in power since 1990, would struggle to win a third term in the October 12 election, New Zealand's first under proportional representation.
The poll showed National unchanged on 35 percent, with three left-wing parties sharing 50 percent between them.
Bolger contrasted his government to the alternative of a "three-headed left-wing coalition" of the Labour Party, economic nationalist New Zealand First and the five party left-wing Alliance grouping.

He described opposition leaders as "the gloom gang". If they won office, Bolger said, unemployment, inflation and interest rates would rise. International investor confidence in New Zealand would evaporate and investment would dry up.
Bolger said Treasury forecasts released last week showed that under National, more national debt could be repaid, taxes cut further and more spent on social programmes.

He told an enthusiastic audience, warmed up by Maori entertainers and -- reflecting Bolger's ancestry -- an Irish dance group, that National needed to get more than 40 percent in the crucial party vote to head off a left-wing government.

Under the mixed member proportional system adopted by New Zealand for this election people vote for local constituency candidates and for a party, but it is the party vote which determines the overall make-up in parliament.
The small free-market ACT and the Christian Coalition are each polling about five percent and by themselves seem unlikely to deliver enough votes to ensure a centre-right government.
Bolger said unlike Labour and the Alliance, which have both ruled out supporting National, he was "ruling no one out and no one in" for post-election deals.

But at an impromptu news conference after the campaign launch he would not specify what National's "bottom-lines" were. "Of course we have to sit down with other parties after October 12, then is the time to negotiate," he said.
"Of course it is not all up for grabs. We have very clear policy positions. Ultimately you can only move forward (policies which have) the support of a majority of the parliament."

In his campaign opening speech Bolger reaffirmed National's commitment to "a decent society" -- the slogan it used in the 1990 campaign which ousted Labour. In a pitch to win back support from the Christian Coalition he harked back to the values instilled in him by his Catholic parents.

As he had in a televised leaders' debate last week, he used a phrase borrowed from U.S. President Bill Clinton, saying National wanted to "build a bridge to the future...wide enough to enable all New Zealanders to cross".
